input: n is the canonical ASCII decimal string for an integer in [1,10^18-1], with length d in [1,18] and no leading zeroes. No Number-valued whole input is accepted. Integer inputs, when present, are primitive safe-integer Numbers excluding negative zero, NaN, infinities, fractions and BigInt. Arrays are dense ordinary Arrays without holes, proxies, subclasses or accessors; strings are primitive. Explicit internal BigInt arithmetic in candidate 564 is a separate declared mechanism. No concurrent mutation or modified standard built-ins are allowed. Preconditions are not checked at runtime. Size bounds do not guarantee available memory or completion within an unqualified runtime budget.
return: A canonical decimal STRING for the nearest nonnegative integer palindrome other than the represented input itself; distance is absolute integer difference and a tie chooses the smaller palindrome. For input 1, the result is 0. The same input, even if already palindromic, is never returned.
mutation_aliasing: All input values, caller containers and ordering remain unchanged. The Solution instance retains no state and separate calls share no mutable result state. A private constant-size candidate Array and short prefix/reflection strings are allocated. No integer result object is exposed to JSON transport; the output is a string.
numeric: Python int and JavaScript BigInt perform every whole-value parse, power of ten, candidate construction, difference, comparison and tie break exactly. Only lengths/indices use Number in JavaScript. Same-width candidates come from prefix-1,prefix,prefix+1; changed-width prefixes are skipped because the two explicit boundaries cover length changes. Candidate values and distances are at most 10^18+1, requiring more than safe Number precision but at most 19 decimal digits. No whole candidate is converted through Number.
complexity: A constant number (at most 5) of candidates are built. String work is O(d) and live string storage O(d); parsing, exponentiation, subtraction and comparison use bounded <=19-digit exact integers and their arithmetic costs are included, not assumed free for unbounded precision. The domain does not claim arbitrary-length big-integer complexity.
